title: Bad Timing
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 31 of 40
content:
Our reservation became three Gems, a cracked windshield, and Greg apologizing to a parking meter. The night a gem emergency ruined our date had its own weather, noises, and opinion about whether I was prepared. I stood in the middle of it with the kind of courage that appears after a person has already said yes. The reflex to run had not vanished because love became possible. It had simply lost the argument for the morning.

The plan was to find out whether disappointment could survive without becoming a verdict. Greg wrote it on a receipt, then copied it onto cleaner paper when he decided the first version looked too much like a confession. Nothing was complicated, which made it frightening. Complicated plans came with exits. This one asked us to notice what we were building while we were building it. I kept my hands busy with streetlights, bent plans, and honest annoyance and tried not to count the ways a good day could become a test.

Greg arrived with one joke already spent and another held in reserve. He was good at making a room less sharp. He was also good at hiding the bruise beneath the joke if nobody asked him to stop. He made a joke about romance being a contact sport, then asked permission to be upset. When he looked at me, the familiar warmth was there, along with the question he was trying not to ask: was I staying because I wanted him, or because I had grown used to being wanted?

I answered by taking an active part in the mess. I said the date could be rescheduled, but the conversation could not be postponed. It mattered to do something that could not be mistaken for passive trust. Greg made space for people so generously that they could forget he needed space too. I did not want to accept his care as an endless resource. I wanted to meet him in the middle, where a hand could be offered and still be allowed to pull back.

The complication was already there: Greg's instinct was to make everyone comfortable, even when he was disappointed. It was not a disaster. Beach City produced problems small enough to laugh at and serious enough to reveal a person. Greg's shoulders tightened. His instinct was to fix the practical thing first, then ask whether anyone had feelings about it. I caught his wrist before he disappeared into the task. He looked down at my hand as if I had interrupted a song.

We talked about the clinic waiting room and our rule about asking. The object was ordinary when it entered our lives, but ordinary things collected meaning when we returned to them. Greg told the story again, leaving out the version where he made himself the fool. He had been young, lonely, and brave in ways he did not know how to name. I was not interested in punishing the person he had been. I was interested in the person beside me now, still learning how to ask.

“A ruined evening is not automatically a ruined relationship.” Greg said, embarrassed by the wisdom of his own sentence.

We took a break without calling it one. Greg found something cold to drink, and I sat where I could see the work waiting for us without being swallowed by it. He told me three small stories about streetlights, bent plans, and honest annoyance: one funny, one embarrassing, and one that ended with him admitting he had been scared. I answered with a truth of my own. The exchange was not dramatic enough for a song, which was exactly why it mattered. Real intimacy kept happening in the unlit spaces between declarations. I could be tired and still be wanted. Greg could be uncertain and still be someone I trusted. We did not have to turn every feeling into a performance before it counted.

I told him what I wanted next. He confused being easy to love with being easy to disappoint. Greg did not rush to reassure me. He did not promise never to fail or never to need more than I could give. He promised to tell me when fear was driving. That was better. A perfect man would have been a stranger. Greg was a person with a van, a guitar, a history of running, and a stubborn desire to come home honestly.

We ate takeout in the van, then kissed without trying to fix the awkwardness. We decided to try again another day.

He set a new date before we finished the noodles. This time, we left enough room for bad timing to be only one part of the story.
